findings.finding: My current finding is that after each round the group of runners with the same score is split exactly in half: the winners (who receive the round’s points) form one half‑size subgroup and the losers form the other half‑size subgroup. Consequently, after the 20 rounds every binary win‑loss pattern of length 20 is assigned to exactly one runner, so all final scores are distinct. The ranking is therefore a permutation of the 2²⁰ runners, and the problem reduces to counting how many permutations can be realized by repeatedly choosing, in each group of size 2ᵐ, a set of 2^{m‑1} “winners’’ that satisfies the necessary prefix condition (no prefix of the sorted speeds contains more winners than losers). This is the core combinatorial constraint that must be satisfied at every round.

My current finding is that the tournament’s pairing rule forces a deterministic partition at each round: in any group of \(2m\) runners the \(m\) fastest must become the winners (receive the \(1\)‑bit for that round) and the \(m\) slowest become the losers (receive the \(0\)‑bit). Consequently each runner’s final 20‑bit score is uniquely determined by his rank among all \(2^{20}\) speeds: the most‑significant bit is 1 iff his rank is in the top half, the next bit is 1 iff his rank is in the top quarter of that half, and so on. Thus the mapping from runners to binary strings (and hence to final scores) is a fixed bijection given the global speed order. This reduces the counting problem to the number of possible speed orderings that can arise from the allowed pairings.

My current finding is that **the tournament forces every final score to be distinct**: after each round the players with a given score are split evenly into winners (who gain the round’s points) and losers (who keep the same score). Consequently after 20 rounds each of the \(2^{20}\) binary strings of length 20 (i.e. the scores \(0,1,\dots ,2^{20}\!-\!1\)) appears exactly once. Thus the only freedom is which runner (ordered by speed) receives which binary string, subject to the rule that in each round the faster half of any equal‑score group must be the winners. This reduces the problem to counting the number of ways to assign the \(2^{20}\) distinct binary strings to the runners while respecting that, at every level of the binary‑tree hierarchy, the faster half of the players in each node receive a ‘1’ at that level. This is the key reduction needed to compute \(N\).

My current finding is that **every bijection between the \(2^{20}\) runners and the \(2^{20}\) binary strings of length 20 can be realized by a suitable choice of pairings in the tournament**.  

Indeed, at round \(i\) the runners are split into groups of size \(2^{20-i+1}\) that share the same first \(i-1\) bits. Since each group contains exactly half with bit \(i=1\) and half with bit \(i=0\), we may arbitrarily choose any subset of size \(2^{20-i}\) in the group to be the winners (receive the 1‑bit) and pair each winner with a distinct loser; this is always possible because we can assign the speeds after the pairings are fixed. Recursively applying this at all 20 rounds yields any desired assignment of the 20‑bit scores, so the number of possible final orderings \(N\) equals the number of bijections, i.e. \((2^{20})!\). Consequently \(k=v_{10}((2^{20})!)\). This reduction to a factorial is the key step.

My current finding is that the number of possible final rankings equals  

\[
N=\prod_{i=0}^{19}C_{2^{i}}^{\,2^{19-i}},\qquad C_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n},
\]

so  

\[
v_{2}(N)=\sum_{i=1}^{19}2^{19-i}=2^{19}-1=524\,287,\qquad
v_{5}(N)=\sum_{i=0}^{19}2^{19-i}\,v_{5}\!\bigl(C_{2^{i}}\bigr)=121\,818.
\]

Hence the largest \(k\) with \(10^{k}\mid N\) is \(k=\min(v_{2},v_{5})=121\,818\), and  

\[
k\bmod 10^{5}=121\,818-100\,000=21\,818.
\]

My current finding is that the total number of possible final orderings is  

\[
N=\prod_{m=0}^{19}\Bigl(C_{2^{m}}\Bigr)^{2^{19-m}},\qquad 
C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
\]

(the Catalan number for each internal node of the binary‑tree tournament).  
Consequently  

\[
v_5(N)=\sum_{m=0}^{19}2^{19-m}\,v_5\!\bigl(C_{2^{m}}\bigr),\qquad 
v_2(N)=\sum_{m=0}^{19}2^{19-m}\,v_2\!\bigl(C_{2^{m}}\bigr),
\]

where \(v_p\) is the exponent of prime \(p\) in an integer (Legendre’s formula gives \(v_p(C_n)=v_p((2n)!)-v_p(n!)-v_p((n+1)!)\)).  
The first few values are  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
m & v_5(C_{2^{m}}) & v_2(C_{2^{m}})\\\hline
0&0&0\\
1&0&1\\
2&0&1\\
3&1&1\\
4&1&1\\
5&0&1\\
6&2&1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots
\end{array}
\]

Thus \(k=\min\{v_5(N),v_2(N)\}=v_5(N)\) and can be obtained by the weighted sum above; the next step is to evaluate this sum (mod \(10^5\)).

My current finding is that the number of possible final rankings equals the number of ways to assign the \(2^{20}\) distinct runners to the \(2^{20}\) distinct binary score‑strings that arise from the tournament.  Because any set of \(2^{19}\) winners can be paired with \(2^{19}\) slower losers (the only requirement is that each winner be matched with a slower runner), every permutation of the runners can be realized as a ranking.  Hence  

\[
N=(2^{20})!
\]

and the exponent of \(10\) dividing \(N\) is the exponent of \(5\) in \((2^{20})!\).  Computing  

\[
v_5((2^{20})!)=\Big\lfloor\frac{2^{20}}5\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\frac{2^{20}}{5^2}\Big\rfloor+\cdots=262\,140 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
k=262\,140,\qquad k\bmod 10^{5}=262\,140-2\cdot10^{5}=62\,140 .
\]

So the required remainder is \({62140}\).

My current finding is that the number of possible final orderings is simply the total number of ways to assign the \(2^{20}\) distinct binary score‑vectors \((b_{1}\dots b_{20})\) to the runners.  
Because at each round we may choose any half of the runners in a score‑group to be the winners, any bijection between the runners and the \(2^{20}\) binary strings (which automatically gives each group exactly half winners and half losers) can be realized by an appropriate choice of pairings and speeds. Hence  

\[
N=(2^{20})!\; .
\]

Consequently the exponent of \(10\) dividing \(N\) equals the exponent of \(5\) in \((2^{20})!\):

\[
k=v_{5}\big((2^{20})!\big)=\Big\lfloor\frac{2^{20}}5\Big\rfloor+\Big\lfloor\frac{2^{20}}{5^{2}}\Big\rfloor+\cdots=262\,140.
\]

Thus  

\[
k\bmod 10^{5}=262140\equiv 62\,140\pmod{100000}.
\]
